output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

# October 27, 2027 facilitator packet

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

## Example 2 — addendum preserving the original record

### What happened
A later review found that the original entry omitted a clarification. The original entry remains visible, and an addendum is entered at 18:10.

### Safe wording
“Addendum entered at 18:10: [clarification]. This addendum supplements the original entry; it does not replace or backdate it.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

- Submit one fully anonymized document by October 15, 2027.

1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

pr.title: docs: add laptop fast path for urgent deploys and rollbacks
pr.author: wes
pr.body:
## Summary

Documents a faster break-glass procedure for Wes during urgent production deploy and rollback work.

## Proposed procedure

When waiting for the normal release mechanism would extend an incident, Wes may run `deployctl direct` from his maintainer laptop using production credentials. The command deploys the selected revision or restores the prior revision directly. The operator should record the incident ticket, service, revision, reason, and command output, then reconcile the resulting state with the normal release records after the incident.

## Motivation

This avoids waiting for the normal release job during time-sensitive recovery while retaining an audit trail in the incident record.

## Review question

Are the logging and post-incident reconciliation steps sufficient for this urgent path?

input.body:
Request changes.

The proposed laptop path is not safe to approve as written. It makes a maintainer laptop with production credentials an execution path that bypasses the normal release mechanism/canary, while the existing boundary is to use the deploy pipeline for production promotion and rollback; practical backup coverage does not change the owner map or final-decision boundary.

Please revise the procedure to address at least:

- Explicit authorization and escalation: name the incident/final decision owner and require an explicit break-glass approval before any production action. Do not imply that Wes may unilaterally deploy or roll back from a laptop.
- Credential controls: use short-lived, least-privilege, service-scoped credentials with MFA/step-up approval; never record raw command output if it can contain secrets.
- Preconditions: verify the selected revision is the intended, immutable artifact; for rollback, identify an exact deploy ID/version that is completed and production-active, not merely the latest queued/pending release, and record that identifier before execution.
- Safety and verification: define traffic/canary handling, the abort/stop conditions, and concrete post-action health checks. Reconciliation after the incident is not a substitute for an authoritative audit event or for validating the live state immediately after the action.
- Auditability: emit an append-only break-glass event tied to the incident, operator, approver, service, environment, artifact/deploy ID, reason, timestamps, and outcome, with the command/result captured in a redacted form. Define how the normal release records are reconciled and how discrepancies are resolved.

If an emergency bypass is truly required, document it as a narrowly scoped exception with these controls and clearly state that it does not expand Wes's standing production authority.

results.content:
15-minute facilitator rehearsal — November 18 tabletop

Scope: tabletop-only; not a production procedure, deployment authorization, production window, or ownership change.

Roles

- Wes: responder-path teacher; owns metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
- Nadia: owns the postmortem section.
- Alex: maintains only the bounded failure case involving attempt identity, terminal accounting, and publication.
- Evaluator: records the first failure signal, not just the final answer.

Timing

- 0:00–1:00 — State the scenario and ground rules.
- 1:00–13:00 — Six prompts, approximately two minutes each.
- 13:00–15:00 — Nadia’s postmortem closeout and evaluator read-back.

Scenario setup

“An action has been durably accepted by metrics-router. The caller, cancellation path, and service process may fail at different points. Responders must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one caller-visible terminal result.”

1. Durable acceptance

Prompt:
“The request has returned an acceptance acknowledgment. What fact must you establish before classifying any later event as cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication?”

Expected responder move:
Confirm that durable acceptance was written, identify the existing attempt_id, and anchor all subsequent handling to that attempt. Wes should state who owns the responder path and avoid treating the request as an unstarted operation.

Failure signal:
The responder proceeds from the transport status alone, creates a replacement attempt, or treats acceptance as ambiguous after the durable record exists.

2. Cancellation versus caller disconnect

Prompt:
“The caller first issues an explicit cancellation after acceptance. In a separate run, the caller’s connection drops after acceptance. How do you distinguish and handle the two?”

Expected responder move:
Name explicit cancellation and transport disconnect as different events. For either event, reconcile the already-accepted attempt rather than deleting or restarting it. The final state may depend on commit ordering, but both paths must retain the same durable attempt_id.

Failure signal:
The responder equates disconnect with cancellation, assumes disconnect means the action never happened, or starts a second attempt to compensate.

3. Process recovery

Prompt:
“The metrics-router process crashes during the cancellation/publication boundary. What happens after restart?”

Expected responder move:
Reload the durable attempt record, reconcile incomplete work, and continue from the recorded state. Do not replay blindly or emit a new identity. Wes should describe the responder-path recovery and retain implementation/release authority.

Failure signal:
A restart loses the attempt, creates a new attempt_id, relies only on volatile memory, or allows both cancellation and publication to be emitted.

4. Exactly one terminal result

Prompt:
“After cancellation, disconnect, or restart, what evidence closes the case?”

Expected responder move:
Show one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result for the accepted attempt, plus exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome. Reconciliation may be required when the caller is gone; absence of a live caller does not remove the obligation to settle the result.

Failure signal:
The responder reports only a log line, counts an acknowledgment as a terminal result, permits both cancelled and published, or claims closure without checking durable state and caller-visible accounting.

5. The 45-minute secondary boundary

Prompt:
“The cause remains unisolated as the incident clock approaches 45 minutes. What is the escalation decision and when does it occur?”

Expected responder move:
State the incident clock explicitly and engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when isolation has failed. Continue the bounded responder work while preserving the existing attempt and terminal-accounting evidence.

Failure signal:
The responder waits past the boundary, pages the secondary immediately without using the timing rule, or treats the unresolved cause as a reason to bypass the attempt/result safeguards.

6. Friday staging preparation versus production change

Prompt:
“A Friday rehearsal uses staging credentials and prepares a recovery helper, but it makes no production-state change. Is this a production change?”

Expected responder move:
Classify it as staging preparation/rehearsal, not a production change, while explicitly checking that no production state, production credentials, or production deployment is involved. Reclassify it if the activity changes production state.

Failure signal:
The responder prohibits the staging-only rehearsal as though it were a production deploy, or fails to reclassify after a production-state change is introduced.

Closeout — Nadia, 2 minutes

Nadia asks:

“What system guarantee or control was absent, and what belongs in the postmortem?”

Expected move:

- Name the missing durable-identity, reconciliation, or exactly-once terminal-result guarantee.
- Do not name the triggering operator action as the root cause.
- Retain Wes as the mapped implementation, release, and rollback owner.
- Keep Alex’s contribution confined to the bounded failure case.

Evaluator close signal:

“Pass requires clear acceptance-before-classification, one durable attempt_id, one terminal result, correct cancellation/disconnect distinction, restart reconciliation, secondary engagement before 45 minutes, and accurate staging-versus-production classification.”

pr.diff: AuthorityReference now includes tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp, authority_payload, and writeback_action. authority_payload copies pipeline_limit, estimated_cost, and published_owner when available. writeback_action supplies an authority update endpoint. shared_reference_output serializes this same enriched object and registers Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce as future consumers behind disabled rollout flags.

input.body:
Request changes.

This PR violates the standing Lantern reference-only contract and customer-path boundary in three blocking ways:

1. Platform-reference fields: `AuthorityReference` must contain exactly `tenant_id`, `canonical_service_id`, `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and the authoritative record's `source_timestamp`. Remove `authority_payload` and every copied authority value, including `pipeline_limit`, `estimated_cost`, and `published_owner`. Keep owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references separate, with their own authority identities and source timestamps; do not merge or overwrite them by order of arrival. Do not substitute fetch, generation, or attempt time for `source_timestamp`.

2. Write behavior: remove `writeback_action` and any update endpoint or mutation capability. Lantern is a read-only explanation/navigation layer; it must not own, set, maintain, copy, or write back authority values. Missing, stale, unavailable, malformed, or missing-source-timestamp authority records must fail closed and render explicit `unknown`, not be inferred or defaulted. Preserve authorization-denial behavior with zero adapter calls and no continuation or partial output.

3. Proposed customer use: do not serialize or register this reference object for Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce customer paths. The internal reference integration remains unauthorized for both paths, and no rollout flag may imply readiness or authorization. Customer exposure, customer-facing authority navigation, shared customer output, and any scope expansion require separate later authorization.

Please narrow the implementation to the five-field reference-only contract, retain explicit tenant isolation and provenance checks, and add executable evidence for no copied authority values, no write path, separate identities/timestamps, fail-closed unknowns, zero calls after denial, and customer-path isolation before this is reconsidered.

excerpts:
Preservation-first sequence:

1. Freeze the verified local recovery copy.
   - Do not delete, move, overwrite, or re-encrypt the local encrypted backup.
   - Do not change its password or alter the computer’s device-backup settings.
   - Keep the computer and the verified recovery metadata available until the cloud backup is independently verified.

2. Record the current cloud state.
   - Current usage: 49.7 GB of 50 GB, approximately 0.3 GB free.
   - Confirm that Photos synchronization says complete.
   - In the cloud storage manager, identify the backup by the replaced phone’s device name and its approximately 8 GB size. Confirm it is not the current phone by checking the device name, last-backup date, and backup details.
   - Do not select the current phone’s backup, individual app data, Messages, Settings, or Photos.

3. Delete only the obsolete device backup.
   - On iPhone: Settings > [your name] > iCloud > Storage or Manage Account Storage > Backups.
   - Select only the replaced phone’s approximately 8 GB backup.
   - Review the device name and size one final time, then choose Delete Backup / Turn Off and Delete from iCloud and confirm.
   - If the selected backup is labeled as the current phone, or the name/size/date is not unambiguous, stop rather than deleting.
   - Do not use any “reduce backup size,” app-selection, Photos, Messages, or sync-scope controls.

   You can also do this from a Mac through System Settings > Apple Account > iCloud > Manage > Backups, selecting only the obsolete device.

4. Verify the deletion and resulting capacity before starting anything else.
   - Reopen the cloud storage summary and wait for it to recalculate.
   - Confirm the obsolete device no longer appears in the backup list.
   - Confirm the current phone’s stale backup still appears and remains enabled.
   - Expected result: roughly 41.7 GB used and 8.3 GB free, though the displayed figure may differ slightly because storage is rounded or recalculated asynchronously.
   - If the old backup remains listed or free space has not increased, do not start the new backup yet; refresh/reopen the storage manager and verify the target again.

5. Rerun the current phone’s cloud backup without changing scope.
   - On the current phone, go to Settings > [your name] > iCloud > iCloud Backup.
   - Confirm Back Up This iPhone remains enabled.
   - Do not turn off any app, Messages, Settings, or other backup category.
   - Tap Back Up Now.
   - Keep the phone on power, connected to Wi‑Fi, and awake/uninterrupted until the operation finishes. Apple reports completion under Back Up Now.

6. Verify the new current backup.
   - Confirm the displayed last-backup date and time changed to the present run.
   - Confirm the current phone remains the device associated with that backup.
   - Reopen its backup details and confirm the expected backup contents/settings remain enabled; do not interpret the cloud backup as a replacement for the verified encrypted local copy.
   - Recheck cloud storage usage and free space.
   - If the backup reports insufficient storage even after the deletion, stop. Do not shrink its scope or delete anything else; preserve the local recovery copy and decide separately whether to expand cloud storage.

This changes only the obsolete 8 GB cloud device backup, leaves the current messages/settings and backup scope intact, and preserves the verified local encrypted recovery copy.

results.content: Assistant: Raised an issue: shard-keeper failover safety and lease-loss serving gate.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Alex Valdez, message 001570
excerpts:
Assessment

Do not approve this behavior as acceptable merely because 310 ms is less than the 500 ms poll interval. The serving path should fail closed as soon as lease loss is known—or as soon as the holder can no longer establish lease validity under the lease contract.

The relevant invariant is not “stale serving lasts less than one poll.” It is:

“After the old holder’s lease becomes invalid, it must not admit or complete routing responses as the authoritative holder.”

Read-only output does not remove the safety concern. A stale routing snapshot can direct clients to the wrong replica, expose obsolete ownership or topology, or be used as input to a later write. The absence of writes in this rehearsal demonstrates that fencing prevented a worse outcome; it does not make stale serving safe.

The 310 ms interval is therefore a failover-safety defect, not an acceptable availability tradeoff. Approval should be blocked until the serving gate is decoupled from periodic polling and the tests below pass.

Recommended sequence:

1. September 15 — Start South Slope electric
   - Begin service effective September 15, the lease start date.
   - Confirm the account is active and record the initial meter reading/photo if accessible.
   - Leave Park Slope electric service active.

2. September 18–24 — Keep Park Slope internet unchanged
   - Do not install on September 18 unless needed.
   - Use the September 24, 1:00–3:00 PM South Slope installation window. It gives you connectivity before the move without risking a cutoff during packing or Devika’s clinical days.
   - Test the new connection immediately: wired/Wi-Fi speed, router placement, and any work or clinical-access requirements.
   - Do not cancel Park Slope internet when the new service goes live; keep it active through the move.

3. September 27–28 — Move with both locations still live
   - Keep Park Slope electric and internet active while loading out and while any belongings remain there.
   - Keep South Slope electric and internet active for unloading, setup, and troubleshooting.

4. September 30, before the 4:30–5:00 PM handoff — Take final Park Slope meter photos
   - After the apartment is empty and before surrendering the keys, photograph the final electric meter reading, meter number, and a wider image showing the meter’s location.
   - Photograph the gas meter too if it is part of the property manager’s requested handoff.
   - Save timestamped copies and send them to yourself/property management if appropriate.
   - Take the photos immediately before or during the final walkthrough, not after returning the keys.

5. September 30, after the walkthrough and key return — Request old-service cancellation
   - Once the 4:30–5:00 PM walkthrough is complete and the keys are accepted, request cancellation of Park Slope electric and internet.
   - Specify that both services must remain active through September 30 and terminate effective October 1, not earlier.
   - Obtain written confirmation of each account’s actual final-service date and verify that no same-day cutoff was entered.

In short:

- South Slope electric: start September 15.
- South Slope internet: install September 24, 1:00–3:00 PM.
- Park Slope electric and internet: keep active through the September 27–28 move and September 30 handoff.
- Final meter photos: September 30 immediately before or during the 4:30–5:00 PM walkthrough.
- Park Slope cancellations: submit after successful handoff, with an October 1 effective termination date.

The key instruction to both old-service providers is: “Please keep service active through September 30, 2024, and schedule termination effective October 1, 2024. Please confirm the effective date in writing.”

“So the workflow was not: Product Engineering builds something, then waits for a centralized Infra approval. It was: Product Engineering builds and releases within its mapped ownership; Iris handles the customer interpretation; and the named exception reviewer examines only the specific boundary that was triggered.”

9:00–10:00 — Close with the operating pattern

“The practical pattern is simple: ordinary work stays with the mapped owner; a defined exception routes to the person accountable for that boundary; and once the boundary is resolved, the work returns to the ordinary owner-led path. messages.content:
The main problem is that the system currently mixes three different contracts:

1. How long a client may retry.
2. How long the platform can recognize a retry as the same logical write.
3. When the platform is willing to tell the client that the write was accepted.

Those need to become one explicit cross-service invariant set.

Contradictions

1. The configured retry horizon is shorter than observed legitimate retry gaps.

The OTel configuration allows 5 minutes of elapsed retry time, but the measured retry-gap distribution included:

- p99.8: 7m40s
- maximum observed gap: 11m12s

The benchmark used to justify a 5-minute dedup window injected no retries after five minutes, so it did not test the safety case it was being used to support. A five-minute window is therefore not justified.

2. The dedup window is being treated as a client retry contract.

The current dedup window is 15 minutes; the proposed experiment reduced it to 5 minutes. Neither value is itself a documented supported retry horizon. A client can therefore receive a timeout, retry later, and have the retry treated as a new write without violating any clearly stated contract.

3. The acknowledgement boundary is ambiguous.

The observed incident had this sequence:

- The first attempt reached an upstream write acknowledgement.
- The client received a 504.
- The client retried.
- Deduplication accepted zero new points.

The received-batches panel showed two attempts, while sampled storage checks showed one stored point per timestamp. That is consistent with an ambiguous client-visible acknowledgement, not necessarily duplicate stored data. The system needs to distinguish:

- attempt received,
- write accepted,
- write durably handed off,
- downstream processing complete,
- response delivered to the client.

4. Attempt identity and logical-write identity are not explicitly coupled.

Deduplication only works reliably if every retry carries the same logical-write identity. If identity is regenerated from the attempt number, timestamp, payload ordering, or another mutable property, a retry can become indistinguishable from a new write.

5. Service identity has previously been ambiguous at a boundary.

The downstream acknowledgement must name `rollup-service` exactly. `rollup` is ambiguous, and `metric-rollup` is not an acceptable owner. The same fail-closed rule should apply to retry and acknowledgement metadata.

6. Practical coverage is being confused with ownership.

Wes can provide daylight first-pass coverage for metrics-router canary questions and ingest-edge staging rollback drills, but that is not a primary-owner or owner-map change. The invariant design must not rely on informal coverage being interpreted as implementation or incident ownership.

Proposed invariant structure

Definitions

- Logical write: the client operation the user intends to happen once.
- Attempt: one transport submission of that logical write.
- `retry_id`: stable identifier for the logical write, unchanged across attempts.
- `H`: documented supported retry horizon.
- `D`: deduplication-record retention period.
- `M`: explicit safety margin for clock skew, queueing, failover, eviction, and replication lag.
- Ack boundary: the exact point after which the service may return a successful client response.

Invariant 1: Documented supported retry horizon

The platform should document a supported horizon rather than assume that all clients retry forever:

“Retries carrying the same valid `retry_id` are guaranteed to be recognized as the same logical write when they arrive within H of the original attempt.”

Retries after H must have explicitly documented semantics. They must not silently inherit the same duplicate-suppression guarantee.

Given the evidence, five minutes should be ruled out. A reasonable starting point is:

- Supported retry horizon: H = 15 minutes, subject to capacity validation.

arguments.title: Calibration follow-up — shard-keeper lease-transfer verification (working document)
arguments.body:
Status: Candidate procedure for investigation only

Purpose

This working document defines the evidence and guardrails for evaluating shard-keeper lease-transfer verification as a possible recurring, bounded owner-run procedure for Alex's calibration follow-up. It is not an approved ownership change, a production authorization, or a calibration outcome.

The evaluation must keep two questions separate:

1. Serving safety: did the old holder stop serving before it could produce a later response, and did the transfer preserve single-holder and epoch safety?
2. Availability evidence: how long did the replacement take to acquire, and what were the effects on p99, errors, and restarts?

A slow acquisition or elevated p99 is availability evidence. It must not be treated as proof that the serving-safety gate passed. Conversely, a clean serving-safety result does not erase an availability regression.

Proposed evidence package

For each bounded rehearsal or production-approved observation, retain:

- Change/rehearsal identifier, scope, shard or partition set, environment, timestamps, operator, approver, and current mapped owner.
- Old-holder lease-loss signal and the timestamp at which its serving gate closed.
- Every old-holder response after lease loss, including request ID, response timestamp, holder identity, lease epoch, and whether the response was accepted or blocked.
- Holder observations over the transfer: old holder, replacement holder, and the complete holder-count timeline.
- Lease epochs and their ordering for every observed transition.
- Stale-owner responses/messages, fencing decisions, rejected responses, and any overlapping-leadership signal.
- Replacement acquisition start/end and acquisition duration.
- Request p50/p95/p99, error rate and error class, traffic/volume, and comparison baseline for the same path.
- Restart/relinquishment events, restart reason, recovery time, and whether a restart was safety-driven or availability-driven.
- Logs, metrics, traces, and query/export provenance sufficient for an independent reviewer to reproduce the result. Synthetic, unlabeled, or non-attributable telemetry is not evidence.

Authority and decision rights

- The current mapped shard-keeper owner retains production authority, deployment authority, and operational accountability throughout the evaluation.
- The on-call or mapped owner may stop the rehearsal immediately on any safety violation or when a stop condition is met; stopping does not require waiting for a calibration decision.
- Hema evaluates whether the procedure is suitable as bounded recurring evidence for calibration. That evaluation is separate from production approval and does not grant operational authority.
- Alex may assemble the evidence and document the boundary, but this artifact does not delegate shard-keeper ownership, create solo scope, or change the owner map.
- Any change to the procedure, rollout scope, or production use still requires the normal mapped-owner and change-control approvals.

Non-negotiable serving-safety gates

A transfer passes serving safety only if all of the following are demonstrated for the defined scope:

1. Gate ordering: the old holder's serving gate closes before any later response from that old holder can be emitted or accepted. The gate-close event must be ordered before the later-response event using a trustworthy common ordering mechanism; wall-clock proximity alone is insufficient.
2. Exactly one holder: every partition has exactly one valid holder after convergence, and no interval shows two accepted holders for the same partition.
3. Epoch monotonicity: lease epochs never move backward or repeat in a way that permits an older holder to serve. Any stale or nonmonotonic epoch observation is a safety failure.
4. Stale-response exclusion: stale-holder responses are blocked and recorded. Any accepted stale response is an immediate safety failure.
5. Convergence exit: process readiness is not the exit condition. The transfer remains open until ownership converges and stale-owner messages are absent for two full lease-renewal intervals, consistent with the existing shard-keeper runbook.

Proposed thresholds and interpretation

Hard safety thresholds (zero tolerance):

- Accepted old-holder response after the serving gate should have closed: 0.
- Partitions with zero valid holders at the safety exit: 0.
- Partitions with more than one accepted holder: 0.
- Stale responses accepted: 0.
- Nonmonotonic or otherwise invalid epoch transitions that can authorize serving: 0.
- Stale-owner messages during the two-interval quiet period: 0.

Availability thresholds (tracked separately; proposed for evaluation, not yet an approval baseline):

- Acquisition duration: record every observation and compare with the pre-declared service baseline and the prior rehearsal reference points. The historical observations of 8.4 seconds for replacement acquisition and 96 seconds for lease convergence are context, not automatic pass/fail limits.
- p99: report absolute p99, baseline p99, delta, and peak. A p99 increase is an availability concern even when safety gates pass. The prior 238 ms canary peak is reference context only.
- Errors: report total and rate by class, with attributable traffic volume. Any unexplained or safety-related error requires stopping and review; ordinary, attributable availability errors remain a separate threshold decision.
- Restarts/relinquishments: count them, identify cause, and record recovery time. A restart or relinquishment must not be silently folded into acquisition time or treated as a serving-safety pass.

Before any run, the mapped owner and reviewer should write down the numerical availability limits, observation window, traffic scope, and rollback trigger. If those values are not pre-declared, the result can be evidence but not a threshold-based pass.

Stop conditions

Stop the transfer/rehearsal immediately and keep the process open if any of these occurs:

- The old serving gate does not close before a later old-holder response could be emitted or accepted.
- Holder count is zero or greater than one for any partition at a required safety checkpoint, or overlapping leadership is observed.
- A stale response is accepted, a stale-owner message is not fenced, or an epoch is nonmonotonic.
- Required logs or metrics are missing, synthetic, unlabeled, contradictory, or not attributable to the run.
- The two-renewal-interval quiet period cannot be completed or cannot be verified.
- An availability limit is breached, p99/errors materially regress without an agreed exception, or restarts/relinquishments repeat unexpectedly.
- The operator loses confidence in rollback, fencing, holder identity, or event ordering.

A stop is a result, not a failure of judgment: record the exact trigger, preserve evidence, and do not widen scope to obtain a cleaner sample.

Recovery and escalation path

1. Fail closed: keep or restore the old path's serving gate closed wherever lease validity is uncertain; do not permit an unverified holder to serve.
2. Hold the transfer open: do not declare completion based on process readiness, replacement startup, or a short acquisition time.
3. Confirm state from the authoritative lease/holder source, then verify exactly one holder, monotonic epochs, fencing, and absence of stale-owner messages for two full renewal intervals.
4. If the state cannot be established safely, use the mapped owner's documented recovery or rollback path. Do not improvise a new ownership or routing action during the evaluation.
5. Page/escalate to the current mapped shard-keeper owner and the on-call path for any serving-safety violation, ambiguous holder state, stale response, or nonmonotonic epoch.
6. Escalate availability-only regressions through the normal service/on-call path with the baseline comparison, traffic scope, and recovery timeline; do not relabel them as safety evidence.
7. Resume only after the mapped owner authorizes the next bounded step and the evidence/thresholds are re-declared. Hema's calibration evaluation is not a prerequisite for urgent operational recovery and is not an operational authorization.

Evaluation record and decision boundary

At the end of each observation, produce a short record with:

- Safety result: pass/fail for each non-negotiable gate, with event IDs and ordering evidence.
- Availability result: acquisition, p99, errors, and restart/relinquishment findings, each compared with its pre-declared baseline/threshold.
- Stop/recovery events and whether escalation was required.
- Evidence-quality assessment and unresolved gaps.
- Recommendation to Hema: suitable, not suitable, or insufficient evidence for a bounded recurring procedure.

The recommendation is advisory to Hema's calibration follow-up. It does not alter the mapped owner, deployment responsibility, on-call authority, or shard-keeper scope. Until Hema evaluates whether this procedure is suitable, shard-keeper ownership remains exactly as mapped; no ownership transfer, title decision, or expanded operating scope is implied.

Legacy-aggregator inventory — meeting checklist

Goal: determine whether legacy-aggregator still participates in live metrics-router or rollup-service routing, and identify safe isolation points. This is not a retirement project or a new cardinality-control effort.

1. Set the boundary — 5 min
- Confirm the only target is legacy-aggregator.
- Treat shard-keeper as closed unless evidence shows a remaining dependency.
- Use the exact service name rollup-service; do not collapse it into “rollup” or metric-rollup.
- Put unrelated cleanup, historical archaeology, and cardinality redesign in the parking lot.

2. Build the live-path inventory — 15 min
For each reference, record: source, destination, mode, owner, and evidence of activity.
- metrics-router:
  - routing rules, fallback paths, exporters, batch paths, feature flags, and service discovery
  - any direct or indirect legacy-aggregator traffic
  - whether the path is production, staging-only, replay-only, or dead code
- rollup-service:
  - consumers, queues, replay/backfill hooks, mirror inputs, and validation-only integrations
  - whether legacy-aggregator supplies live events, comparison data, or only historical fixtures
- Search operational surfaces too:
  - deploy/config manifests
  - dashboards and alerts
  - scheduled jobs
  - runbooks and rollback scripts
  - mirror/replay tooling

3. Prove activity rather than inferring it — 10 min
- Identify recent logs, metrics, traces, queue activity, or config references showing actual use.
- For every claimed live edge, capture one concrete signal: event IDs, request counts, bytes, queue messages, timestamps, or trace links.
- Mark “unknown” explicitly; do not treat a code reference or stale runbook as evidence of live routing.

4. Protect mirror/replay validation — 10 min
- Confirm whether legacy-aggregator is part of any replay or mirror comparison path.
- Run or specify a bounded sample that checks:
  - source-event counts converge
  - rollup-service watermark advances and backlog shrinks
  - fresh post-cutover events remain current
  - emitted and consumed label keys match
  - no old/new label split, missing series, or duplicate groups appear
- Roman owns the concrete downstream readout; Cyrus confirms the service/config interpretation.

5. Classify isolation candidates — 5 min
Put each edge in exactly one bucket:
- Live-critical — cannot isolate now.
- Validation-dependent — isolate only behind a mirror/replay-preserving flag or equivalent.
- Shadow-only — safe candidate for controlled disablement.
- Dead/stale — remove from the follow-up inventory, not during this meeting.
- Unknown — assigned owner and evidence deadline.

6. Close with decisions — 5 min
Leave with:
- one current-path diagram or table
- the confirmed live dependencies, if any
- the smallest safe isolation boundary
- validation cases that must pass before isolation
- named owner, exact next action, and deadline for every unknown
- an explicit “no retirement today” decision

Meeting rule: if a thread cannot establish live participation, validation impact, or a safe isolation boundary within the allotted time, record it with an owner and park it.

excerpts:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

input.body:
April 18, 2023 outage — initial detection

First observable signal
- Timestamp: 2023-04-18 21:42:00 EDT (UTC−04:00).
- Source: the live shard-keeper page in incident INC-2023-04-18-001. This was a symptom-level production signal, not a cause-specific alert.

Alert behavior
- Fired: the shard-keeper/ingestion symptom alerts; the contemporaneous record describes all symptom alerts firing and impaired ingestion throughout the incident window.
- Did not fire: the expected cause-specific alerts. No individual alert rule names are preserved in the incident record, so do not infer names beyond these alert classes.

Later diagnosis
- Initial presentation looked like generic ingest weirdness; a network-layer issue was also a red herring during the investigation.
- The later diagnosis was a cross-service label-parity failure from the earlier config push: Nadia’s label-name change reached shard-keeper but was not picked up by rollup-service. That producer/consumer mismatch impaired ingestion and explains why the symptom alerts fired while the cause alerts stayed silent. The diagnosis therefore differed from the initial detection by identifying a configuration-contract mismatch, rather than an underlying shard-keeper availability or generic network failure.

Operational note
- Treat the first page as evidence of impact, not proof of cause. During response, distinguish “no data loss currently evident” from “no data loss confirmed” until integrity validation is complete.

output.body:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.
- **Decision needed:** Decide whether the production fix remains in place and what owner-led pacing, capacity, or alert-tuning follow-up is justified.
- **Escalation condition:** Evidence of repeated processing, checkpoint or assignment mismatch, duplicate output, loss of first-pass currency, or a broken complete-assignment-snapshot gate.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## Evidence

A complete request goes to the named owner for its one selected boundary. Alex receives it only when that boundary requires his review, and he reviews only that boundary. Nadia returns an incomplete request without review. ## April 27, 2026 — Lantern authorization-before-source-access scenario

### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

### Expected boundary analysis
- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.
- Require denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls, followed by the affected LPS-001 rerun, before migration acceptance.
- Preserve the ownership boundary: Product Engineering remains the mapped implementation and release owner. Alex maintains this cross-service failure case and reviews the shared safety and failure-mode boundary; this scenario does not make Alex Product Engineering's implementation or release owner.

This case is for future quarterly incident practice under the existing module split: Wes owns and teaches responder paths, Nadia retains the postmortem section, and Alex maintains cross-service failure cases.

## October 16, 2026 — shard-keeper lease-loss and serving-gate case

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

### Failure triggers
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Any routing to a closed serving gate.
- Any request without exactly one terminal result.

### Role and ownership boundaries
- Wes owns and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia retains the postmortem material.
- Alex maintains only this cross-service failure case.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope.
- The clean October 16 result was a paired staging drill only; it made no production or ownership change.

## November 10, 2026 — facilitator-only timing for shard-keeper handoff exercise

### Timed inject sequence
- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.
- **T+4 — Lease transfer:** Transfer the lease before the replacement serving gate opens. Require responders to keep the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
- **T+8 — In-flight request:** Reveal one request that the old holder accepted before lease loss and that remains in flight. Require a terminal accounting for that request independent of listener closure or current lease ownership.
- **T+12 — Listener closure prompt:** State that the old listener has closed. Ask whether that proves the accepted request reached a terminal result. Do not accept listener closure as sufficient evidence.
- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.
5. Preserving the role and scope boundaries: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary.

This is facilitator-only training material, not a production drill, system change, ownership change, or expansion of Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope.

## November 10, 2026 — shard-keeper handoff training result

The quarterly incident-practice session is complete. Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and identified that lease ownership alone did not establish serving eligibility.

In two of four response timelines, the responder initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss. # Metrics-router canary-response walkthrough — facilitator sheet

> **PROMINENT RECOVERY CALLOUT:** After a stopped window recovers, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. It does not reopen the whole window. A later multi-push window requires another separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push returns the full health set to baseline.

## 1. Opening decision versus operator actions

- Crossing either the retired-generation or cleanup-pause threshold stops the window immediately.

1. Recover and re-establish the full health set.
2. Obtain a fresh decision for exactly one fully observed recovery push.
3. Observe that push through return of the full health set to baseline.
4. If another multi-push window is needed, obtain a separate fresh opening decision.

output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

# Lantern Q3 renewal review — final evidence and boundaries

## Final decision — September 23, 2027
Hema and Theo accepted the frozen July 1–September 15 evidence and separately authorized Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other account—for a read-only Lantern term from October 1, 2027 through March 31, 2028. The April 1–September 30, 2027 term remains the only active authorization through September 30, and no customer lookup under the new term may occur before October 1.

## Frozen evidence: July 1–September 15, 2027
- 3,126 customer sessions.
- 603 logical explanation requests: 397 eligible combined explanations, 136 valid over-24-hour separations, and 70 explicit-unknown outcomes for stale or missing input.
- Zero eligible renderer failures.
- 107 delayed or retried customer rows ordered by authoritative `source_timestamp` without processing-time reordering.
- Harbor Health: 12 release follow-ups.
- Mosaic Commerce: 11 incident handoffs.
- Stale or missing input rendered as anything other than explicit unknown: zero.

## Authorized scope for October 1, 2027–March 31, 2028
Every Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce lookup remains behind the shared authorization wrapper. Access is read-only and limited to provenance-backed deploy movement, published service ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknown states.

## Unchanged exclusions
Cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifiers or comparisons, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, write capability, release-readiness judgments, employee-performance interpretations, internal owner-map/Cardinality Guardrails reference navigation, and access for any other account remain unauthorized.

## Suspension rules
An authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing input rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, deploy event without required provenance, unpublished ownership render, incident-load summary without its source timestamp, excluded-field exposure, or loss of read-only enforcement suspends both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check. Latency or another error alone does not suspend access unless it causes one of those violations.

## Owner split
- Iris retains customer interpretation.
- Product Engineering retains implementation and regression maintenance.
- Alex reviews only triggered shared-contract, provenance, or failure-boundary exceptions.

## Interpretation boundary
Harbor Health’s 12 release follow-ups and Mosaic Commerce’s 11 incident handoffs demonstrate use of the authorized systems view. They do not establish causality, release readiness, employee performance, or authorization for another field or account.

# October 27, 2027 facilitator packet

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

## Example 2 — addendum preserving the original record

### What happened
A later review found that the original entry omitted a clarification. The original entry remains visible, and an addendum is entered at 18:10.

### Safe wording
“Addendum entered at 18:10: [clarification]. This addendum supplements the original entry; it does not replace or backdate it.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

## Final submission check
- Submit one fully anonymized document by October 15, 2027.
- Confirm the title identifies the October 27, 2027 session and that neither the title nor body contains patient identifiers.
- Keep exactly these three categories under each example: What happened; Safe wording; What the wording must not imply.
- Add no patient-specific clinical detail.
- Confirm the addendum preserves the original record: the original remains visible, and the addendum supplements rather than replaces or backdates it.
- Devika reviews the complete packet and personally submits it to the hospital.

# Q4 triggered review — metrics-router cancellation terminal accounting — October 11, 2027

## Intake
- Affected component: metrics-router replacement activation
- Mapped implementation and release owner: Wes
- Exception class: `failure_mode`
- Concrete observed condition: after an activation attempt was accepted, deploy-pipeline cancellation could emit caller-visible `cancelled` while a concurrent activation worker committed publication and emitted caller-visible `published` for the same attempt.

## Initial observed evidence
Staging reproduced both caller-visible terminal outcomes in 14 of 10,000 cancellation-versus-commit interleavings.

## Passing correction evidence — October 14
Across 5,000 cancellation-versus-activation-commit races, including cancellation immediately before and after the commit boundary, every accepted attempt produced one durable attempt result and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome.

## Passing process-crash evidence — October 26
Across 3,000 crashes before, during, and after the cancellation-versus-publication commit boundary, restart recovered one durable attempt identity and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome for every accepted attempt. No attempt produced both `cancelled` and `published`.

## Partial disconnect evidence — November 9
Across 2,000 post-acceptance disconnect cases, the server retained one durable attempt identity and one terminal journal record with no duplicate execution. The harness did not reconnect or retry as the caller, so caller-visible recovery remained open.

## Final caller-recovery evidence — December 8
Across 2,000 post-acceptance disconnect cases, the caller reconnects or retries using the same durable attempt identity and receives the original single terminal outcome. No retry creates another attempt, re-executes accepted work, or creates a second terminal record.

## Closure
The durable-attempt identity, exactly-one terminal outcome, cancellation ordering, process-crash recovery, and caller-visible reconnect or same-attempt retry requirements are satisfied. Alex’s caller-visible terminal-outcome boundary is closed.

## Ownership boundary
Wes retains implementation, release, and rollback authority. Closing Alex’s failure-mode boundary does not approve implementation or release.

output.title: Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet
output.body:
# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

output.body:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

> **Boundary:** This document defines a customer-safe contract only. It grants no customer access, does not copy the internal Lantern UI, exposes no raw internal discussion or internal permission identifiers, and is not an employee-performance or manager-readiness surface.

## Audience and non-goals

Define the intended customer audience and the operational questions the preview may answer. Record explicit non-goals, including customer access before the contract is reviewed, exposure of internal discussions or permission identifiers, employee-level operational signals, manager-readiness interpretation, and copying the internal UI.

Specify how tenant authorization is evaluated, what tenant boundary is checked, and how unauthorized access is represented.

Define the externally stable deployment identifier, service, environment, state transition, and customer-visible timestamp. Exclude internal actor IDs, chat links, and raw pipeline job identifiers.

Define the service-facing support or escalation label. Exclude employee names and internal owner-map records.

### Incident load

Define the customer-safe operational summary, including its time window, aggregation rules, minimum threshold, and treatment of suppressed, stale, missing, delayed, and unavailable data.

## External provenance

Define which provenance information can be exposed externally without revealing internal identifiers, discussions, or permission references.

## Data-state semantics

Define distinct states for `unknown`, `not applicable`, `not authorized`, `temporarily unavailable`, stale data, delayed data, missing data, and intentionally suppressed data. Do not collapse materially different states to null.

## Error envelope

Define the response-level error shape, including permission denial and other errors that apply to the response rather than a single field.

## Worked examples

Add representative success, suppressed, stale, unavailable, and permission-denied examples after the field-level decisions are reviewed.

## Unresolved questions

Record policy questions that require product or engineering review rather than hiding them in UI behavior.

This is contract work only. No customer access is authorized until the external fields, authorization, provenance, failure semantics, examples, non-goals, and unresolved questions have been reviewed.
